Strong induction proves a property for every natural number at or above the base case by assuming the property holds for every value strictly below n, rather than only for n minus one. The professor's framing on the slides is that this is a convenience and not a stronger axiom: any proof written with strong induction can be rewritten as ordinary induction over a modified predicate. The base case is not a formality. A proof with a false base case establishes nothing at all, however clean the inductive step looks on the page. In my own notes I wrote that the inductive hypothesis is the thing you are allowed to assume, and the inductive step is the obligation you still owe. That framing is what makes the difference between the two forms obvious: ordinary induction hands you one previous case, strong induction hands you all of them. Use the strong form when the recursion in the problem reaches back more than a single step, which is the usual situation for divide and conquer recurrences.

**Check this:** the slides say the base case must be verified separately for every residue class when the step size exceeds one; my notes say a single base case suffices. The slides are authoritative here.
